shots.narration: Every fungus on this list has taken over something alive,
and a few have started on people.
Today, each one gets a turn with Doug.
Doug did not agree to this.
Insects.
Massospora.
Periodical cicadas spend thirteen or seventeen years underground,
then climb out all at once for about a month of singing and mating,
and Massospora is waiting for them.
Spores left in the soil by an earlier generation infect the young cicadas as they dig their way up.
On an insect about the length of a paperclip,
the fungus eats away the lower half of the abdomen from the inside.
The joints between the last few segments break,
and those segments simply drop off, leaving a chalky white plug made entirely of spores.
The disturbing part is that the cicada doesn't stop.
It keeps flying around and trying to mate, and every landing shakes spores onto the next cicada in line.
It isn't dying.
It's delivering.
Infected males even start flicking their wings the way females do when they're ready to mate,
so healthy males come straight to them and leave covered in spores.
Chemists have also found cathinone inside infected cicadas,
a stimulant related to amphetamine, and the researchers think it may help keep the insects going while they fall apart.
Massospora is built for cicadas and can't infect people,
which is exactly why Doug is dressed as a cicada.
Doug kept waving at the other cicadas
while the back of his costume popped off like a cork.
He didn't notice.
The bird did.
Doug has died. Again.
Seventeen years underground, one month in the sun, and the fungus gets the rest.
Death-Pose Fly Fungus.
Its scientific name is Entomophthora muscae,
but the people who study it usually recognise it by something simpler:
the exact pose its flies are found dead in.
In a lab study, infected flies died four to seven days after they were exposed,
and on the final day they made their last move in the five hours before sunset.
The fly climbs to a high spot and presses its mouthparts against the surface,
where a sticky droplet glues it in place.
Then, in small bursts, its wings lift up and away from its body,
and it dies exactly like that.
In the lab, about nine out of ten dying flies raised their wings this way.
Doug has met a fungus like this before, when an ant fungus made him climb a plant in his parasite days.
This one adds an alarm clock.
About five hours after sunset, the fungus breaks out through the body in pale bands and starts firing spores.
Each one leaves at about ten meters per second,
close to the average speed of Usain Bolt's world-record hundred meters.
The worst part is what the fungus does with the body next.
On dead female house flies, the fungus gives off a blend of chemicals that draws in healthy males.
They try to mate with the dead, infected female,
and that close contact is exactly how they catch it.
The fly fungus doesn't infect people either, hence the fly costume.
Doug climbed the window at sunset,
raised his wings,
and was very proud of the pose.
He held it permanently.
Doug has died. Again.
It doesn't only kill the fly, it turns the body into bait for the next one.
The Cave Spider Fungus.
In twenty twenty-one, a BBC crew was filming the nature show Winterwatch at Castle Espie,
a wetland reserve in Northern Ireland, when a volunteer looked up.
On the ceiling of an old Victorian gunpowder store was a spider coated in white fungus.
DNA tests later showed that nobody had ever described this fungus before.
Viewers of the BBC's Springwatch nicknamed it Gibellula bangbangus, after the gunpowder store.
In January twenty twenty-five, scientists gave it a proper name, Gibellula attenboroughii, after David Attenborough.
It infects orb-weaving cave spiders.
The bigger of the two known hosts has a legspan of around five centimeters,
about the height of a credit card, and both species normally keep to dim, damp places.
Here's the eerie part.
The infected spiders leave their webs and hiding spots and walk out onto open ceilings and walls to die.
Out in the open, where air moves and other spiders pass by, the spores have a better chance of spreading.
The researchers suspect the fungus is steering the spider, the way some fungi steer ants,
but nobody has proven that yet.
Since then, more infected spiders have turned up on cave roofs and walls across Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland.
Old records also hint at similar spider die-offs in parts of England and Wales.
Its whole genus attacks only spiders, so Doug is a spider.
Doug left his web and strolled across the ceiling to say hello to everyone.
Everyone could see him.
That was the idea.
Doug has died. Again.
A spider that lives in the dark walked into the open to die, for a fungus nobody had even named.
Whole species.
Chytrid.
Every fungus so far has taken one animal at a time,
but this one is counted in species.
Chytrid lives in the skin of frogs, toads and other amphibians,
which is a bad place for a fungus to be, because frogs drink and breathe partly through their skin.
The fungus wrecks how that skin moves salts.
In a study on green tree frogs, salt transport across the skin dropped by more than half,
the salts in the blood fell, and in the end the heart simply stopped.
Genetic studies trace the outbreak strain to the Korean peninsula.
It began spreading in the early twentieth century, around the same time the global trade in amphibians took off,
and it rode that trade around the world.
Here comes the part that's hard to say out loud.
A major study in twenty nineteen linked chytrid to the decline of at least five hundred and one amphibian species.
That's roughly six and a half percent of every known amphibian,
or more than three cards out of every fifty-two card deck.
Ninety of those species are presumed extinct,
and only about one in eight of all the declining species shows any sign of recovery.
The study's authors called it the greatest recorded loss of biodiversity caused by a disease.
Other scientists have challenged how that count was made, and the authors have defended it.
It isn't killing frogs.
It's deleting kinds of frog.
Chytrid isn't known to affect humans, which is why Doug is a frog.
Doug sat in a perfectly clean pond and read a pamphlet about how clean it was.
The water really was clean.
Doug has died. Again.
Nobody had to poison the pond, because the fungus came in riding on the frogs.
White-Nose Syndrome.
In February twenty oh six, a caver about forty miles west of Albany, New York,
photographed hibernating bats with something white on their noses,
and noticed several dead bats nearby.
The white was a fungus called Pseudogymnoascus destructans.
It loves the cold, and it grows on the muzzles, ears and wings of bats while they hibernate
and can't do anything about it.
A hibernating bat lives on a fixed amount of stored fat, and that fat has to last the whole winter.
Even healthy bats wake up now and then over the winter, and every wake-up burns fat.
Bats with this fungus wake up far more often, and the more they wake, the sooner the infected ones die.
A government study found infected bats burned twice as much energy over the winter as healthy ones did.
It's like heating your house all winter on half a tank of fuel.
The catch is that the fungus doesn't have to kill the bat directly.
It just keeps waking it up until the bat runs out.
By twenty twelve, biologists estimated it had killed at least five point seven to six point seven million bats in North America.
Three species have dropped by more than ninety percent,
and by twenty twenty-three, the disease had reached forty states and eight Canadian provinces.
That same year, the northern long-eared bat was reclassified as endangered.
No human illness has ever been linked to it, which is what the bat costume is for.
Doug hung upside down and set his alarm for spring.
It went off in January.
Then again.
Then again.
Doug has died. Again.
He didn't die of the cold, he died of getting up too often.
People.
Valley Fever.
The costumes come off now,
because every fungus from here on can reach people, starting with one that lives in the dirt.
Valley fever is caused by a fungus called Coccidioides,
which lives in the soil of dry areas in the southwestern United States, Mexico, and parts of Central and South America.
People catch it by breathing in spores from dust.
The spores are tiny, about two to five micrometers long,
so more than a dozen of them, lined up end to end, would fit across a single human hair.
Here's the twist.
On January seventeenth, nineteen ninety-four, the Northridge earthquake hit Southern California.
It set off landslides in the mountains near Simi Valley,
and those landslides threw up huge clouds of dust that drifted down into the towns below, with the spores inside them.
Over the next eight weeks, Ventura County recorded two hundred and three cases,
roughly ten times what doctors would normally expect,
with the most new cases appearing about two weeks after the earthquake.
More than half of them were in Simi Valley, and people caught in the dust clouds had about three times the odds of being diagnosed.
It was the first outbreak of its kind ever reported after an earthquake.
Valley fever doesn't spread from person to person, so every one of those cases came straight out of the dust.
Three people died.
Doug stood in the middle of the dust cloud in a hard hat and coughed exactly once.
Doug is fine.
About sixty percent of people infected never have any symptoms at all, and never know they had it.
Doug is most people.
An earthquake shook a fungus out of a mountain and into a county's lungs.
Ergot.
For most of history, nobody knew this was a fungus, so people just ground it up and ate it.
Ergot is a fungus that grows on rye,
and it replaces the grain with a hard spur, dark purple to black, sitting right where the kernel should be.
Some spurs are only a couple of millimeters long, while others grow to about ten times the size of a normal grain.
At harvest, the spurs ended up in the grain,
and the outbreaks hit hardest among people who lived largely on rye bread.
People called the illness holy fire, for the burning it caused,
and later Saint Anthony's Fire, after an order of monks founded in ten ninety-five to care for its victims.
That order went on to build more than three hundred and seventy hospitals.
Between the years nine ninety and eleven thirty, an estimated fifty thousand people or more died of it in southern France alone.
The unsettling part is that for centuries, the poison was the bread, and nobody could see the difference.
In nineteen seventy-six, a researcher proposed in the journal Science that ergot might explain the Salem witch accusations.
That same year, two other researchers replied in the same journal that the evidence didn't support it,
and many historians remain unconvinced.
Ergot did leave something useful behind.
Chemicals from it became medicines, including one still used for migraine and one used to control bleeding after childbirth.
Doug bought a fresh loaf at the market
and ate half of it on the spot,
announcing it was the best bread he had ever had.
Doug has died. Again.
Somewhere in that loaf was a black spur that looked exactly like a grain.
The Tomb Fungus.
King Casimir the Fourth of Poland died in fourteen ninety-two,
the same year Columbus first sailed across the Atlantic,
and he was laid to rest in a tomb in Wawel Cathedral, in Kraków.
The tomb stayed sealed for nearly five hundred years.
In nineteen seventy-three, a team of about a dozen researchers opened it,
and according to later accounts, ten of them died within weeks.
The newspapers called it the curse of the king.
Later investigations found a mould in the tomb called Aspergillus flavus,
and that mould has been blamed for the deaths.
Aspergillus flavus is not exotic at all.
It's the same mould that can grow on stored peanuts and corn,
and its spores can cause lung infections, mostly in people whose immune systems are already weak.
But here's the strange part.
The curse fungus is now a lead for a cancer drug.
In twenty twenty-five, scientists at the University of Pennsylvania pulled a new family of molecules out of Aspergillus flavus
and named them asperigimycins.
In lab dishes, two of them had strong effects against leukemia cells,
and one modified version did about as well as two drugs already used to treat leukemia.
The same compounds did little or nothing to breast, liver or lung cancer cells.
So far that's only in the lab, on cells, with animal testing next, and it's a long way from a cure.
Doug opened the tomb wearing a paper crown and said,
"hi king?"
Nothing happened at all.
Doug is fine.
We had high hopes for this one, but the curse, it turns out, was mostly a newspaper headline.
Cryptococcus gattii.
Until the late nineteen nineties, this fungus was mostly known from tropical and subtropical regions,
often around eucalyptus trees in places like Australia.
Then, starting in nineteen ninety-nine, people and animals on Vancouver Island, off the west coast of Canada, began falling ill with it.
The animals included dogs, cats, ferrets, porpoises, llamas and even a horse,
and some were found before the first human cases.
Scientists went looking and found it living on Douglas fir trees,
in the soil around them, and even floating in the air and the water.
It wasn't passing through.
It had moved in,
and scientists still can't say for sure whether it arrived recently or had been there unnoticed all along.
Here's the problem.
Most dangerous fungi go after people whose immune systems are already weak,
and this one also infects healthy people.
On Vancouver Island, the yearly rate came to about twenty-five cases per million people,
which is roughly one person a year from every sold-out crowd at Wrigley Field.
British Columbia has the largest reported group of people infected with it anywhere in the world.
From nineteen ninety-nine to two thousand seven, British Columbia recorded two hundred and eighteen cases and nineteen deaths.
It didn't stay on the island, either.
Cases have since turned up on the British Columbia mainland and in Washington and Oregon.
Doug went for a nature walk
and hugged the biggest tree on the trail.
"Hi friend?"
Doug has died. Again.
It was a tropical fungus, it moved somewhere cold, and it didn't wait for anyone to get sick first.
Candida auris.
In two thousand nine, scientists in Japan described a new yeast taken from a patient's ear
and named it after the Latin word for ear.
At the time, it looked like a footnote.
Then it showed up in South Asia, South Africa and South America at almost the same time.
Genetic testing showed these weren't one strain spreading around the world,
but separate groups that had appeared on their own, on three continents, all at once.
Most strains resist at least one main type of antifungal drug, and some resist all three.
It survives on surfaces and objects for a long time,
and it spreads easily between patients in healthcare facilities.
In twenty nineteen, the Centers for Disease Control put it on its list of urgent threats,
and in twenty twenty-two, the World Health Organization put it in its critical priority group.
In the United States, clinical cases went from four hundred and seventy-six in twenty nineteen to one thousand four hundred and seventy-one in twenty twenty-one.
To see why this one matters, you need to know about the wall.
Our bodies sit at about thirty-seven degrees Celsius,
and most fungi simply can't grow that warm.
When researchers tested nearly five thousand fungal strains,
every one-degree rise between thirty and forty degrees shut out about six percent more of them.
That heat is one big reason mammals rarely get fungal infections.
When it was first described, Candida auris grew well at forty degrees.
That's hotter than our bodies, and about as hot as safety regulators say a hot tub should ever get.
And here's where it gets personal.
One hypothesis says it learned to handle that heat out in the world,
adapting to warmer temperatures as the climate warmed, until our bodies were no longer too hot for it.
It's only a hypothesis, and the researchers say it will be hard to prove.
Our body heat has been a wall against fungi for millions of years.
This might be the first one learning to climb it.
Doug turned his thermostat up to thirty-seven degrees,
on the theory that nothing could stand it.
Something sat down beside him.
Doug has died. Again.
The cap has outlived one hundred and forty-seven Dougs,
and as of today, it is also food.
Doug deaths: one hundred and forty-seven.
Which fungus on this list would you least like to meet?
Tell us in the comments.
